newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, facing strikes, set to leave sanatorium.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, facing strikes, set to leave sanatorium.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, facing miners' strikes and problems with the 1997 budget, is set to move to a country residence soon, almost exactly a month after undergoing major heart surgery.

Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying that the move from the sanatorium where Yeltsin has been recovering could take place on Wednesday -- although it could also be later than that.
Both the sanatorium and the country residence are located in a compound of government buildings at Barvikha, a village set in woodland to the west of the Russian capital.

Yeltsin, 65, held a regular meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday to talk about a European security summit held earlier this week and about Russia's 1997 budget plans, due to be discussed by parliament on Friday.
The Russian Foreign Ministry hailed the two-day summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) as a triumph for its ideas on future European security.
"The main result of the summit is that our idea for creating a new model of European security is winning ever more support," a ministry statement said.
"In spite of everything our vision of European architecture in the 21st century...is forging its way ahead."

But the optimistic tone of the statement contrasted to the reception for the Russian team at the summit, which failed to win support for a proposal to develop the OSCE into a powerful security body and a counterweight to the Western NATO alliance.
Chernomyrdin returned home to a row about the budget and about a strike by miners, who helped Yeltsin to electoral success in 1991.
Now, impoverished by economic reforms and bitter at mounting wage arrears, they want his government to quit.
Many of the miners say they have not been paid for months and they blame the government for the web of wage and tax arrears, one of Russia's biggest social and economic problems.
Union officials said 400,000 miners were taking industrial action on Wednesday, the second day of the strike. But coal company Rosugol said only 61,000 mine workers had downed tools.
"I cannot imagine how trade unions could say that as many as 400,000 miners were on strike," a Rosugol spokeswoman said.

Interfax news agency said Chernomyrdin and Yeltsin had decided to send First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin to the main mining region -- the Siberian district of Kuzbass -- to talk to the miners there.
The president, who had his operation on November 5, has not yet addressed the Russian people and has been shown only rarely on television since the surgery, a quintuple bypass.

Another economic problem facing the government is the fate of Russia's 1997 budget draft, due to be debated by the State Duma lower house of parliament on Friday at a meeting which Chernomyrdin is expected to attend.

The chamber is dominated by communists and their allies and deputies have already rejected the draft once, complaining that revenue plans are unrealistic and spending forecasts do not take the needs of the poorest Russians into account.
The communist speaker of the Duma said on Tuesday that the parliament might approve a budget for three months "so the government's hands are not tied".

The government is trying hard to rake in extra tax revenues to meet the terms of a loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund and has threatened companies with bankruptcy if they do not pay their bills.
